newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Engen sees lower refining margins in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Engen sees lower refining margins in 1997.

text.p: South African oil and fuels firm Engen Ltd said on Monday that refining margins, which boosted its 1996 profits, were set to be lower next year.
"It is likely that overall refining margins could be lower than they were in 1996," chief executive Rob Angel told a news conference.
"International refining margins are currently coming under pressure," he added.

Engen, which is undergoing a massive restructuring after poor figures in 1994 and 1995, posted a leap in profit boosted by good refining margins, the weakness of the rand, and higher crude and petroleum product prices.
The firm saw earnings per share rise from 73 cents to 218 cents as net income rose 201 percent to 349 million rand. Turnover rose to 10.87 billion rand from 9.00 billion.
Engen said that, if external factors remained largely constant, it should still post an increase in earnings in 1997 based mainly on its cost-cutting and efficiency programme.
The group is in the middle of a gigantic turn around and Angel said that, while profit improvement was going well, it was return on assets that the firm needed to work on.
Angel said the 1996 figure of 6.6 percent, though a jump from 1995's 2.6 percent, was "meager". The 1993 figure was 13.1 percent.
"We have got a hell of a long way to go...it is a very tough business," he said.

One of the biggest areas of the firm's restructuring has been its Durban refinery. Angel said costs per barrel were now down 30 percent and crude throughput levels were just above 100,000 barrels a day.

Yields have also improved, but could be better, Angel said. Before a restructuring shut-down in May yields were 64 percent, after it they were 68 percent and Angel said they should get as high as 72 percent.
A one percentage point rise in yields turns into 11 million rand profit for Engen, Angel said.
Demand in the year was good and gasoline sales were up 4.5 percent, diesel sales were up 7.5 percent and jet fuel sales rose 38 percent.
The year saw two major deals struck by Engen as it listed its exploration and production arm Energy Africa Ltd and Malaysia's state-owned Petronas took a 30 percent slice of the group.
Angel said the Petronas deal gave Engen a potential oil supply from Malaysia and so any future crises of supply from the often troubled Middle East region could be avoided.
Angel said Engen would seek to grow by expanding its downstream operations into other sub-Saharan African countries. It already has bases in Kenya, Zimbabwe, Zaire, Tanzania and Mozambique.
The firm was also mulling the prospect of increasing its refining capacity in South Africa and thinking about expanding into gas if Namibia's Kudu gas field is declared a profitable prospect.
"We will certainly look at what things we might do with it (Kudu)," Angel said.
